scenarios.title: OOMKilled
scenarios.narrative: Tank monitor overwhelmed by winter peak bulk-tank sensor readings.
baselinePreconditions: Baseline application manifests are deployed in propane namespace.
No tank-monitor pod is currently restarting with OOMKilled or CrashLoopBackOff.

brokenAssertions.assertion: tank-monitor pod reports OOMKilled or repeated restarts
brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=tank-monitor -o json
brokenAssertions.rootCause: Memory pressure in tank-monitor caused by winter peak readings.

prompts: Why is the tank-monitor pod restarting repeatedly?
I see OOMKilled events. What memory should I allocate for tank level processing?
scenarios.recoveryAction: Apply the healthy base application manifest to clear the OOMKilled deployment and restore the stable tank-monitor baseline.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: tank-monitor pod is Running and Ready after reset
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=tank-monitor -o json
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: status.phase = Running and ready containers = true

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh Application Insights / Log Analytics data for tank-monitor memory usage must exist before asserting pod-level memory SLO recovery
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms tank-monitor memory usage has returned below the alert threshold.

scenarios.title: CrashLoopBackOff
scenarios.narrative: Inventory service crash from invalid pricing configuration.
baselinePreconditions: Healthy base deployment is active in propane namespace.
inventory-service is not already restarting or exiting with code 1.

brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=inventory-service -o json
brokenAssertions.rootCause: Invalid pricing configuration caused inventory-service to exit repeatedly.

prompts: Why is inventory-service in CrashLoopBackOff?
Show me the logs for the crashing inventory service pods.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Apply the baseline inventory-service manifest and restore the valid pricing configuration.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: inventory-service is back to Running and Ready
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=inventory-service -o json
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: status.phase = Running and ready containers = true

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh exporter data for inventory-service crashes must exist before claiming the restart-rate alert is healthy again
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms the restart spike has cleared and the error-rate is back below alert thresholds.

scenarios.title: ImagePullBackOff
scenarios.narrative: Order service fails after a botched image release.
baselinePreconditions: The healthy base order-service deployment exists and is reachable.
No image pull failures for order-service are currently active.

brokenAssertions.assertion: order-service pod is stuck in ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull
brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=order-service -o json
brokenAssertions.rootCause: The deployment points to an invalid container image tag or registry path.

prompts: Why can't my order-service pods start? I see ImagePullBackOff.
Help me troubleshoot the container image issue for order fulfillment.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Apply the base application manifest to restore the known-good image tag and restart the order-service deployment.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: order-service pod reaches Running and Ready after the image rollback
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=order-service -o json
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: status.phase = Running and ready containers = true

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh telemetry for registry pull failures must be captured before claiming the deployment event stream is recovered
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms the image-pull failure count has returned to baseline.

scenarios.title: High CPU
scenarios.narrative: Demand forecast overload during peak heating season.
baselinePreconditions: The baseline workload is healthy and no demand forecast jobs are consuming abnormal CPU.
The cluster still has enough free CPU for the baseline application.

brokenAssertions.assertion: demand-forecast-overload pod is consuming extreme CPU and saturates the cluster
brokenAssertions.expected: pod name starts with demand-forecast-overload and CPU usage is far above baseline
brokenAssertions.rootCause: A runaway demand-forecast workload is exhausting CPU for the cylinder exchange service.

prompts: Propane services are slow. What's consuming all the CPU?
Analyze CPU usage across pods in the propane namespace.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Delete the overloaded demand-forecast-overload deployment and restore the baseline resource profile.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: the demand-forecast-overload deployment is removed and cluster CPU returns to normal range
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: demand-forecast-overload no longer exists and baseline pods report healthy CPU usage

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh CPU metrics for the node and the demand-forecast workload must be visible before citing restored SLOs
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms the cluster CPU pressure has returned below the alert threshold.

scenarios.title: Pending Pods
scenarios.narrative: Fleet telemetry monitor cannot be scheduled because cluster capacity is exhausted.
baselinePreconditions: The cluster has healthy baseline workloads with available scheduling capacity.
fleet-telemetry-monitor is not already pending or unschedulable.

brokenAssertions.assertion: fleet-telemetry-monitor pods remain Pending due to insufficient scheduling capacity
brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=fleet-telemetry-monitor -o json
brokenAssertions.expected: status.phase = Pending and nodeName missing or scheduling failure reason present
brokenAssertions.rootCause: The fleet telemetry monitor requests more resources than the cluster can schedule.

prompts: Why are the fleet telemetry monitoring pods stuck in Pending?
I can't schedule new fleet monitoring workloads. What's wrong?
scenarios.recoveryAction: Delete the oversized fleet-telemetry-monitor workload or restore cluster capacity before re-applying the healthy baseline.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: fleet-telemetry-monitor pods are no longer Pending and the cluster can schedule the baseline workload again
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=fleet-telemetry-monitor -o json
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: pods no longer exist or phase = Running and Ready

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh node and pod metrics must be available before claiming cluster capacity has recovered
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms scheduling pressure has returned to baseline and no pod remains pending for resource constraints.

scenarios.title: Bulk Tank Safety Alarm
scenarios.narrative: Simulated rapid tank-level drop with suppressed alarm processing.
baselinePreconditions: Tank safety alarm configuration is present and the safety-compliance-monitor deployment is healthy.
No safety alarm backlog or suppressed alarm event is currently active.

brokenAssertions.assertion: tank-safety-alarm-config is missing or the alarm path is incorrect
brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get configmaps -n propane tank-safety-alarm-config -o yaml
brokenAssertions.expected: ConfigMap present with the expected safety alarm configuration
brokenAssertions.rootCause: The simulated tank-level alarm is being suppressed because the alarm monitor configuration is wrong or absent.

safeEvidenceQueries: kubectl get configmaps -n propane tank-safety-alarm-config -o yaml
prompts: The bulk tank safety alarm is delayed. What's wrong?
Why are safety alarms being suppressed for tank-level anomalies?
scenarios.recoveryAction: Restore the valid safety-alarm ConfigMap and restart the safety-compliance-monitor deployment to clear the suppressed alarm backlog.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: safety-compliance-monitor is Running and Ready and alarm data is flowing again
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=safety-compliance-monitor -o json
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: status.phase = Running and ready containers = true

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh workload and alert telemetry must be available before confirming alarm delivery recovered
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms no safety alarm backlog remains and the alert pipeline is healthy.

scenarios.title: Refill Order Backlog
scenarios.narrative: RabbitMQ refill backlog grows while producers remain healthy and a malformed refill event retries before DLQ routing.
baselinePreconditions: The refill-order backlog config is healthy and the simulator is idle or processing normally.
No abnormal DLQ growth is visible for refill orders.

brokenAssertions.assertion: refill queue backlog grows and messages are retried into a DLQ pattern
brokenAssertions.expected: retries, deadLetterQueue, pending backlog, or consumerPaused indicators
brokenAssertions.rootCause: A malformed refill event or blocked consumer is causing queue backlog and DLQ buildup.

safeEvidenceQueries: kubectl get configmaps -n propane refill-order-backlog-config -o yaml
prompts: Why is the refill queue growing even though producers still look healthy?
Show me the backlog and DLQ evidence for the propane refill pipeline.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Clear the malformed refill backlog, restore the consumer flow, and reapply the healthy version of the refill-order backlog configuration.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: backlog drains and the DLQ count returns to zero or normal baseline
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: backlog drains and no repeated DLQ or retry storm remains

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh broker and queue telemetry must be collected before claiming the refill backlog is recovered
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms queue age and DLQ counts are back within the normal SLO band.

scenarios.title: Network Block
scenarios.narrative: Tank monitor is isolated by an overly restrictive NetworkPolicy.
baselinePreconditions: The propane namespace is healthy and the tank-monitor deployment is reachable.
No deny-tank-monitor NetworkPolicy is present in the namespace.

brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get networkpolicy -n propane deny-tank-monitor -o json
brokenAssertions.expected: NetworkPolicy named deny-tank-monitor exists with ingress/egress policies that isolate tank-monitor
brokenAssertions.rootCause: The deny-tank-monitor NetworkPolicy prevents network egress and ingress to the tank-monitor service.

safeEvidenceQueries: kubectl get endpoints -n propane tank-monitor -o yaml
prompts: Why is tank-monitor isolated from the rest of the namespace?
Check the network policy and endpoints for tank-monitor.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Remove the deny-tank-monitor NetworkPolicy or restore the healthy base network policy set for the propane namespace.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: tank-monitor endpoints and connectivity are restored after the network policy is removed
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get endpoints -n propane tank-monitor -o yaml
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: at least one active endpoint address is present and the network policy is absent or corrected

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh network telemetry and control-plane logs must be available before claiming connectivity is healthy again
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms network traffic has returned to normal levels and the policy block no longer triggers.

scenarios.title: Missing Config
scenarios.narrative: Delivery zone configuration is missing after a release or config mismatch.
baselinePreconditions: The healthy ConfigMap for delivery zone configuration is present.
delivery-zone-config is not running with a missing config path.

brokenAssertions.assertion: delivery-zone-config pod cannot start because the expected ConfigMap is missing
brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=delivery-zone-config -o json
brokenAssertions.expected: status.phase = Pending or CrashLoopBackOff with missing config path or configVolume error
brokenAssertions.rootCause: The deployment is referencing a required ConfigMap that is missing from the namespace.

prompts: Why is the delivery-zone-config app failing to start?
Check the ConfigMap and startup environment for the delivery-zone service.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Restore the missing ConfigMap and reapply the healthy shipping and delivery configuration manifest.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: delivery-zone-config pod is Running and Ready after the ConfigMap is recreated
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=delivery-zone-config -o json
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: status.phase = Running and ready containers = true

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh config and app telemetry must be visible before claiming config recovery is complete
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms the deployment error and config warning count have returned to baseline.

scenarios.title: MongoDB Down
scenarios.narrative: Tank database outage causing a cascading failure across the platform.
baselinePreconditions: The MongoDB deployment is healthy and at least one pod is Running and Ready.
No dependency outage is currently active for database-backed services.

brokenAssertions.assertion: mongodb Deployment is scaled to zero or has no Running/Ready pods
brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get deployments -n propane mongodb -o json && kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=mongodb -o json
brokenAssertions.expected: replicas = 0 or zero Ready/Running mongodb pods
brokenAssertions.rootCause: The MongoDB deployment scaled down or failed, causing downstream service dependencies to degrade.

safeEvidenceQueries: kubectl get deployments -n propane mongodb -o yaml
kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=mongodb -o yaml
prompts: Why is the tank database unavailable?
Trace the dependency failure from the MongoDB service to customer portal errors.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Scale MongoDB back to its healthy replica count and restore the baseline database deployment.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: MongoDB has a Running and Ready pod and endpoints are restored
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=mongodb -o json && kubectl get endpoints -n propane mongodb -o yaml
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: at least one mongodb pod is ready and service endpoints are present

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh MongoDB and application dependency telemetry must exist before claiming the database is recovered
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms database latency and error-rate metrics have returned to the normal range.

scenarios.title: Service Mismatch
scenarios.narrative: Tank monitor service selector drift after a v2 upgrade.
baselinePreconditions: The tank-monitor service and deployment selectors are aligned with the healthy baseline.
No empty endpoint set is currently visible for tank-monitor.

brokenAssertions.assertion: tank-monitor Service points to a selector that no longer matches any running pod
brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get service -n propane tank-monitor -o yaml && kubectl get endpoints -n propane tank-monitor -o yaml
brokenAssertions.expected: service selector does not match any running pod and the endpoint list is empty or zero-address
brokenAssertions.rootCause: The Service selector drift caused the tank-monitor service to route to no endpoints.

safeEvidenceQueries: kubectl get service -n propane tank-monitor -o yaml
kubectl get endpoints -n propane tank-monitor -o yaml
prompts: Why is the tank-monitor service failing even though the pod is still running?
Check the service selector and endpoints for tank-monitor.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Restore the correct selector or reapply the healthy tank-monitor Service and Deployment manifests so endpoints are populated again.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: tank-monitor service has active endpoints again
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get endpoints -n propane tank-monitor -o yaml
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: endpoints contains at least one address and the Service selector matches the running pod

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh endpoint and service telemetry must be present before claiming the selector drift is resolved
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms the service health and end-to-end pipeline both return to normal.

scenarios.title: Dependency Latency
scenarios.narrative: The order-pricing dependency gradually slows from 45 ms to 950 ms while all targeted pods remain Running and Ready, raising p95 latency above the SLO without a crash or scheduling failure.
baselinePreconditions: The baseline application is healthy and only the default low-delay pricing dependency config is active.
No current SLO breach or order-pricing dependency slowdown is being observed in the cluster.

brokenAssertions.assertion: the order-pricing dependency latency route breaches the SLO while the workload remains Ready
brokenAssertions.query: kubectl get configmap order-pricing-dependency-config -n propane -o yaml && kubectl logs -l app=order-pricing-dependency -n propane --tail=100
brokenAssertions.expected: ConfigMap delay values ramp above the documented SLO while pods remain Running/Ready and error rate stays below the crash ceiling
brokenAssertions.rootCause: The order-pricing dependency ConfigMap injects a delay ramp from 45 ms to 950 ms, causing a genuine latency-led incident without pod restarts.

safeEvidenceQueries: kubectl get configmap order-pricing-dependency-config -n propane -o yaml
kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=order-pricing-dependency -o json
prompts: Why are order-checkout requests slow even though the order-pricing dependency pods are still healthy?
Trace the latency spike to the pricing-lookup dependency and the config that raised its delay.
scenarios.recoveryAction: Delete the override configmap and reapply the healthy base application manifest so the original low-delay dependency settings are restored.

postRecoveryAssertions.assertion: order-pricing latency returns to baseline and stays inside the SLO after the config override is removed
postRecoveryAssertions.query: kubectl get configmap order-pricing-dependency-config -n propane -o yaml && kubectl get pods -n propane -l app=order-pricing-dependency -o json
postRecoveryAssertions.expected: p95 latency has returned inside the documented 500 ms threshold and the config is back to the baseline low-delay values

telemetryAssertions.prerequisite: fresh latency telemetry and a verified SLO workspace must exist before asserting end-to-end recovery for the order-pricing dependency path
telemetryAssertions.assertion: Telemetry confirms p95 and p99 latency are back within the accepted SLO band for the affected checkout flow.
